ne-e54d7172.stem: Which thalamic nucleus relays sensation from the face (trigeminal nerve) and taste fibres to the cortex?
ne-e54d7172.explanation: The trigeminal lemniscus and the taste fibres from the solitary nucleus end in the VPM; the medial lemniscus and spinothalamic fibres from the body end in the VPL. Thalamic lesions may cause contralateral hemianaesthesia and thalamic pain (Dejerine–Roussy).

ne-48237eed.stem: Which hypothalamic nucleus mainly synthesises antidiuretic hormone (ADH)?
ne-48237eed.explanation: ADH is made mostly in the supraoptic and oxytocin mostly in the paraventricular nucleus; both are carried along axons to the neurohypophysis. The suprachiasmatic nucleus regulates the circadian rhythm, the ventromedial nucleus satiety and the lateral hypothalamus hunger.

ne-1cff0e6f.stem: Which hypothalamic structure is characteristically damaged in Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome (thiamine deficiency)?
ne-1cff0e6f.explanation: In chronic alcoholism and thiamine deficiency the mammillary bodies, the medial thalamic nuclei and the periaqueductal grey matter are damaged. Disruption of the Papez circuit explains Korsakoff amnesia and confabulation.

ne-afe9b56a.stem: A newborn's head circumference is growing rapidly. MRI shows enlarged lateral and third ventricles with a fourth ventricle of normal size. Where is the obstruction most likely?
ne-afe9b56a.explanation: CSF passes from the lateral ventricles through the foramen of Monro into the third ventricle, through the aqueduct of Sylvius into the fourth ventricle, and from there through the foramina of Magendie and Luschka into the subarachnoid space. If the third ventricle is enlarged and the fourth normal, the block is in the aqueduct (congenital aqueductal stenosis).

ne-25e1a0ce.stem: Where is cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) mainly produced and where is it absorbed?
options: Produced in the choroid plexus, absorbed through the arachnoid granulations into the dural venous sinuses.
Produced by ependymal cells, absorbed into lymphatic vessels.
Produced in the arachnoid granulations, absorbed in the choroid plexus.
Produced in the pia mater, absorbed in the central canal.
Produced in the choroid plexus, absorbed in the fourth ventricle.
ne-25e1a0ce.explanation: In adults about 500 ml of CSF is produced a day; about 150 ml is present at any one time. Absorption occurs mostly through the arachnoid granulations projecting into the superior sagittal sinus. Impaired absorption causes communicating hydrocephalus.

ne-37bdea3f.stem: A patient has ptosis, mydriasis and a down-and-out deviation of the right eye together with weakness of the left arm and leg. Where is the lesion most likely?
options: Medial part of the left medulla oblongata
Ventral part of the left midbrain
Ventral part of the right pons
Ventral part of the right midbrain (Weber syndrome)
ne-37bdea3f.explanation: In Weber syndrome the oculomotor fibres and the cerebral peduncle are affected together in the ventral midbrain: third nerve palsy on the same side, hemiparesis on the opposite side. Because the corticospinal fibres cross in the medulla, brainstem lesions give 'crossed' signs.

ne-3d7055ab.stem: A patient with sudden vertigo and nausea has loss of pain and temperature on the left face and the right trunk and limbs, hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, a left Horner syndrome and left-sided ataxia. Tongue movements are normal. Which artery is occluded?
options: Left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (or left vertebral artery)
ne-3d7055ab.explanation: In lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome the spinal trigeminal nucleus (same-side face), the spinothalamic tract (opposite-side trunk), the nucleus ambiguus (dysphagia, dysphonia), the descending sympathetic fibres (Horner), the vestibular nuclei and the inferior cerebellar peduncle are involved. The medially placed nucleus of XII is spared.

ne-81f72625.stem: Which of the following is NOT expected in medial medullary syndrome (anterior spinal artery occlusion)?
options: Loss of pain and temperature on the same side of the face
Atrophy of the tongue muscles on the same side
Loss of proprioception and vibration on the opposite side
Deviation of the protruded tongue towards the side of the lesion
ne-81f72625.explanation: The medial medulla contains the pyramid (contralateral hemiparesis), the medial lemniscus (contralateral loss of deep sensation) and the hypoglossal nerve (ipsilateral tongue palsy). The spinal trigeminal nucleus lies in the lateral medulla and is affected in Wallenberg syndrome.

ne-443079d7.stem: The motor nucleus of which of the following cranial nerves lies in the pons?
ne-443079d7.explanation: III and IV have their nuclei in the midbrain; V (motor), VI and VII in the pons; IX, X and XII in the medulla. The nuclei of VIII lie at the pontomedullary junction.

ne-8ecd7107.stem: Which structures form the facial colliculus in the floor of the fourth ventricle?
options: The abducens nucleus and the facial nerve fibres looping around it
Hypoglossal nucleus and dorsal nucleus of the vagus
Vestibular nuclei and cochlear nerve fibres
ne-8ecd7107.explanation: Within the pons the facial motor fibres loop around the abducens nucleus (internal genu) and raise a bulge in the floor of the fourth ventricle. A lesion here causes ipsilateral palsies of VI and VII together.

ne-5da8a287.stem: A patient sways from side to side when standing and walking and walks with the feet wide apart, but has no clear dysmetria when sitting and using the arms. Where is the lesion most likely?
ne-5da8a287.explanation: The vermis and paravermal zone coordinate the trunk and axial muscles; a lesion causes truncal ataxia and a broad-based gait (for example from alcohol). Hemispheric lesions cause dysmetria, intention tremor and dysdiadochokinesia in the limbs on the same side.

ne-aa74e926.stem: Which structure carries the fibres from the pontine nuclei to the cerebellum (pontocerebellar fibres)?
ne-aa74e926.explanation: The middle cerebellar peduncle (brachium pontis) is the largest peduncle and consists entirely of pontocerebellar (afferent) fibres. The superior peduncle mainly carries fibres leaving the cerebellum (efferent), and the inferior peduncle carries fibres from the spinal cord and the olive.

ne-d50b404c.stem: Which cell is the only output neuron of the cerebellar cortex and is inhibitory (GABAergic)?
ne-d50b404c.explanation: The axons of Purkinje cells go to the deep cerebellar nuclei (dentate, emboliform, globose, fastigial) and the vestibular nuclei and inhibit them. The main output of the cerebellum is through the deep nuclei, the largest being the dentate nucleus.

ne-05903053.stem: Where do most corticospinal fibres cross?
options: At the lower end of the medulla oblongata (decussation of the pyramids)
In every segment of the spinal cord
ne-05903053.explanation: About 85–90% of corticospinal fibres cross at the lower end of the pyramids and form the lateral corticospinal tract. The uncrossed fibres descend in the anterior corticospinal tract and cross at segmental level.

ne-6d09f28c.stem: After basilar artery thrombosis a patient is fully conscious but cannot move their arms, legs or face and cannot speak. They can only move their eyes up and down and blink. What is this condition?
options: Coma – lesion of the reticular activating system
ne-6d09f28c.explanation: A ventral pontine lesion interrupts the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts; because the reticular formation in the dorsal pons is spared, consciousness is preserved. Vertical eye movements and blinking are controlled by the midbrain and so are preserved.

ne-0a8db49c.stem: Which reddish nucleus in the midbrain receives fibres from the cerebellum?
ne-0a8db49c.explanation: The red nucleus receives fibres through the superior cerebellar peduncle and influences the flexors of the upper limb through the rubrospinal tract. Its rich blood supply and iron content make it look pinkish in a fresh section.

ne-8a618879.stem: In adults, at what level does the lower end of the spinal cord (conus medullaris) usually end?
ne-8a618879.explanation: Because the vertebral column grows faster than the spinal cord during development, in adults the conus medullaris lies at L1–L2 (about L3 in the newborn). Below it are the cauda equina and the filum terminale. The dural sac ends at S2.

ne-c6fa7ddb.stem: Which is the most suitable and safe interspace for lumbar puncture in adults?
ne-c6fa7ddb.explanation: The line joining the highest points of the two iliac crests (Tuffier's line) passes roughly through the spinous process of L4. Because the cord ends at L1–L2, a needle inserted at L3–L4 or L4–L5 only pushes aside the roots of the cauda equina.

ne-f7851598.stem: In a lumbar puncture, which is the last ligament the needle passes before entering the epidural space?
ne-f7851598.explanation: The needle passes in turn through skin, subcutaneous tissue, the supraspinous, interspinous and flavum ligaments into the epidural space, then through the dura and arachnoid into the subarachnoid space. Loss of resistance at the ligamentum flavum guides epidural anaesthesia.

ne-6dcbddb7.stem: A patient stabbed in the back has motor paralysis and loss of deep sensation (vibration, position) below T10 on the right, and loss of pain and temperature starting about T12 on the left. What is the lesion?
options: Hemisection of the left half of the cord
Hemisection of the right half of the cord (Brown-Séquard syndrome)
ne-6dcbddb7.explanation: In a hemisection the corticospinal tract (motor paralysis) and the dorsal column (deep sensation) are affected on the same side. Because pain and temperature fibres cross 1–2 segments above their entry, loss of pain and temperature appears on the opposite side, starting a few segments below the lesion.
